transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Dale Willman.
The Supreme Court handed a major defeat to Missouri Republicans Friday in a redistricting
case that could help determine control of Congress.
As NPR's Nina Totenberg reports, the case involves a Republican-friendly map that the
High Court had already rejected.
Missouri's Secretary of State, at the urging of President Trump, sought to use a redistricting
plan adopted in 2025, but the state Supreme Court ruled the move unconstitutional and
the U.S. Supreme Court agreed, twice.
After contrary rulings from two lower federal courts, the High Court, for the third time
and with definitive language, told Missouri to cease and desist.
The justices noted that they have repeatedly cautioned against lower courts altering election
rules on the eve of an election, and in fact, voting in Missouri has already begun.
Nina Totenberg, NPR News, Washington.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is returning to Israel after a brief visit
to New York to address the United Nations General Assembly.
As NPR's Kat Lonsdorf reports, his speech was defiant and defensive, as Israel appears
increasingly isolated on the world stage.
As Netanyahu stepped up to the podium, dozens of diplomats in the audience stood and walked
out.
Netanyahu then referred to them as "moral cowards."
He celebrated and defended the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, and defended Israel against much
of the criticism from many world leaders this week, calling them "tyrants."
Several accused Israel of genocide in Gaza, a claim Netanyahu rejected.
The combative address comes as Netanyahu faces a tight election next month that will decide
if he remains Prime Minister.
His U.N. address was largely viewed as a campaign speech back home.
Netanyahu met with very few world leaders while in New York, and notably not President
Trump.
Kat Lonsdorf, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Pope Leo is adding his voice to the rising concern over the rapid introduction of artificial
intelligence.
Speaking at the UNESCO headquarters in Paris Friday, the pontiff said those fears are real.
"Without a shared ethical foundation, the many channels of communication risk multiplying
false information and giving currency to words devoid of meaning, thereby hindering dialogue
rather than fostering it.
Artificial intelligence amplifies this problem."
Leo said he welcomes an initiative by UNESCO to promote the responsible use of media and
digital tools, including AI.
New Jersey's Democratic Lieutenant Governor resigned Friday.
He was being pushed to leave by the state's governor over accusations of ethical lapses
and inappropriate behavior with women.
Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell denies the charges.
He says he suspects he's being scrutinized because he's a black single man.
He's a Methodist pastor and a former university president.
You're listening to NPR News.
The National Weather Service is warning residents along the mid-Atlantic coast of possible flooding
as a powerful nor'easter sits off the coast this weekend.
Dangerous conditions are expected for the next several days with potential flooding from
heavy rains, and massive waves are already pounding some sections of the coast.
Ferry services to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket have also been disrupted.
Alabama has reached a settlement with TikTok in a lawsuit that claimed a social media company
designed its platform to be addictive to kids and misled consumers about it.
M.P.S.
John Ruach has more.
TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama $100 million, and that figure could go up to $300 million
if certain conditions are met.
A statement from Alabama's attorney general says the short video platform also agreed
to implement a series of safety features designed to protect children.
Those include a two-hour daily time limit extendable by parents, pauses that interrupt
teens using the platform continuously, restrictions on nighttime access, and a prohibition on
cosmetic filters for teen users.
The TikTok agreement follows a similar settlement last month between the social media giant
META and a group of states that case also hinged on whether the social media platforms
were designed to hook kids and whether the company was truthful to the public about it.
John Ruach, NPR News.
College football analyst Tim Tebow says he's pausing his relationship with the Christian
organization LifeSurge.
The group has been accused of using predatory sales tactics to exploit its followers' faith
and financial insecurity.
Tebow won the 2007 Heisman Trophy.
He's made tens of thousands of dollars speaking at LifeSurge events to promote their products.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.

topics.text: Supreme Court rejects Missouri redistricting plan for third time, siding against Republicans
Israeli PM Netanyahu delivers defiant UN speech as diplomats walk out in protest
Pope Francis warns of artificial intelligence risks at UNESCO headquarters in Paris
New Jersey Lieutenant Governor Dale Caldwell resigns over ethical lapses and behavior accusations
Powerful nor'easter off mid-Atlantic coast threatens flooding and disrupts ferry services
Alabama settles lawsuit with TikTok over addictive platform design targeting children
College football analyst Tim Tebow pauses relationship with Christian organization LifeSurge
